During AB testing, stakeholders rejected Option 1, which required an extra click to view services, and chose Option 2's immediate detail display instead, trading a denser first screen for one less click between a resident and a real answer.

artifacts.intro: Journey maps, lived-experience archetypes, and system maps aligned partners around whole-person, participatory navigation design.

desktopMotion.body: The public home page doubles as the front door: category tiles and a needs-assessment prompt let residents start from a known category or a guided question, no account required.

metrics.label: Crisis-Response Speed
metrics.note: Faster interventions reached residents in active behavioral-health crisis sooner.

metrics.label: Referral Completion
metrics.note: More residents who started a referral completed the connection.

metrics.label: Assessment Navigation Ease
metrics.note: Most residents reached the assessment on their first try.

reflection.body: Treating stigma as a design constraint, not a footnote, worked: 119 structured interviews across 13 workgroups surfaced barriers that engagement data alone never would have caught, and it paid off directly in a 47% drop in crisis-response time and 35% more completed referrals. Building trust into the SDoH screener before ever optimizing its funnel is what made both numbers possible in the first place. If I could revisit just one decision, I'd have built the provider dashboard and referral tracking alongside the resident-facing screener from day one, instead of phasing it entirely into Next Steps — the personal spreadsheets driving provider-side fragmentation were as urgent as anything residents themselves were facing.
nextSteps: Next, we're expanding the Provider Dashboard with referral tracking and outcome measurement to improve accountability and service follow-through, and integrating health records for seamless coordination between county systems and providers.

We're developing culturally responsive access through a Spanish-language interface and tailored resource categories, and building a mobile app optimized for offline use so residents in low-connectivity areas aren't locked out of care.

hero.statement: AI design democratizing diamond valuation for miners

overview.body: In Sierra Leone's artisanal mining communities, information asymmetry lets middlemen undervalue rough diamonds by 30 to 70 percent, while professional tools like DiamondMaster and Sarine's scanners demand gemological training, paid subscriptions, and steady internet most miners lack. Diamond Valuation AI, built and shipped as the Root Ally app, replaces that gatekeeping with a smartphone scan, online or offline, that returns an AI-generated market value in minutes. Working closely with Root Studios, Pact, and GIA, I led the participatory research and interface design for miners with limited technical literacy, shifting valuation power from centralized middlemen toward the miners who actually hold the diamonds.
overview.disciplines: Participatory Design Research, Computer Vision Interface Design, Offline-First Mobile Architecture, Field Research, Cross-Functional Team Collaboration.

problemContext.problem: Diamond valuation has always favored buyers: in Sierra Leone's artisanal mining communities, information gaps let middlemen undervalue rough stones by 30 to 70 percent through local pricing networks miners have little power to question. Professional alternatives were no better fit. DiamondMaster and CARATRATE require gemological training and paid subscriptions, and Sarine's scanning technology assumes stable internet and centralized facilities, none of which remote mining sites reliably offer. The less visible constraint was trust, not technology: miners already carried cellphones capable of running an app, but decades of exploitation by centralized valuation systems left mistrust that any new tool would need to overcome, plus security risk in traveling to prove it wrong.
problemContext.brought: I led mixed-methods research and participatory workshops with 25 artisanal miners in Sierra Leone to surface the exact barriers artisanal miners were facing, then designed a mobile-first, offline-compatible AI interface using computer vision to translate gemological complexity into visual, low-literacy interactions. I also directed cross-functional collaboration between Root Studios, Pact, and GIA to keep the resulting valuation tool decentralized and genuinely accessible.

approach.blurb: My approach starts from the idea that most systems are built to be exclusionary, and a designer's role is to democratize systems that marginalize vulnerable communities, prioritizing accessibility, transparency, and immediate value for miners the market previously excluded.

accordion.title: Baseline Information
accordion.body: Early fieldwork in Kono confirmed what mattered most: miners already carried smartphones, but technical literacy varied widely and trust in any centralized system was low. Traditional valuation tools served dealers, not miners, requiring expertise and subscriptions no artisanal miner could justify. Even professional options like Sarine's scanning technology stayed out of reach, and security concerns ruled out centralized valuation facilities entirely as a fix.

accordion.title: Research & Strategy
accordion.body: I ran a mixed-methods study combining contextual interviews across mining sites with participatory workshops involving 25 miners, following Participatory Technology Development principles rather than researching at a distance. Those sessions surfaced real scanning workflows and pain points directly from the people who'd use the tool, while parallel collaboration with gemological experts helped distill professional-grade valuation principles into interactions simple enough for anyone to follow.

accordion.title: Summary of Findings
accordion.body: Miners understood diamonds better than the system gave them credit for, but their knowledge was fragmented: they could describe basic qualities without connecting them to market value or cutting strategy, the exact gap local pricing networks exploited to undervalue stones by 30 to 70 percent. Limited technical literacy, intermittent connectivity, and deep mistrust of centralized systems compounded that gap, reinforcing the same power imbalance the whole project set out to break.

accordion.title: Defining Design KPI's
accordion.body: Three strategic pillars became our project-level goals: a simplified, visual-first interface requiring minimal technical knowledge, so limited literacy stopped being a barrier to entry; an offline-first architecture delivering full scanning functionality with no internet connection, matching the connectivity miners actually have; and a single unified AI system merging viewing, imaging, and pricing that previously required separate specialists miners couldn't access.

accordion.title: Prototyping & Implementation Strategy
accordion.body: Miners tested early wireframes and experience flows directly in the field, which surfaced a clear need for stronger visual guidance during scanning and value reports built for mining-site conditions, not office reviews. Later prototypes added real-time visual guidance, automated value estimation, and downloadable reports miners could use in price negotiations. Current work focuses on optimizing the offline AI model so it holds up without connectivity.

artifacts.intro: Theory of Change, stakeholder maps, and pain-scale analysis grounded the design in miners' realities.

desktopMotion.body: A desktop walkthrough would follow one rough stone end to end: a miner scans six angles, watches AI analysis resolve into a value, then submits verified provenance to ROOT.

metrics.label: Miner Empowerment
metrics.note: Miners gained real confidence to negotiate instead of underpricing.

metrics.label: Miners Reached
metrics.note: Artisanal miners gained direct access to fair-market valuation tools.

metrics.label: Fair-Value Increase
metrics.note: Miners captured more of their diamonds' true market worth.

reflection.body: Treating trust as the product, not an afterthought, worked: grounding the interface in 25 participatory workshops before writing code is what got miners past decades of centralized exploitation, and it shows in the numbers, a 70 percent empowerment rate and a 40 percent lift in fair value captured. Starting from miners' own fragmented knowledge, rather than assuming ignorance, made an AI valuation tool feel trustworthy instead of just another outside system. If I could revisit one decision, I'd have scoped the ROOT submission flow, provenance plus media of the miner, into the first pilot instead of an afterthought, since verifying who found a stone matters as much as pricing it fairly.
nextSteps: Next, we're deploying a pilot with 100 to 200 miners to field-test the offline AI model under real mining conditions.

We're establishing a local valuation hub through Root Foundation so adoption doesn't depend on one app session, and building visual-first training programs that grow miners' own negotiation confidence.
Longer term, we're also exploring the same decentralized approach for gold and coltan mining.

hero.statement: Provoking collective joy inside anonymous city spaces

overview.body: In dense cities like New York, 52 percent of residents regularly feel lonely despite constant physical proximity to millions of strangers. As lead researcher, I worked with Theo Walcot to build Memory Tubes, golden tube installations using research-through-design methods, deploying provocative prompts across high-traffic spaces to interrupt New York's typical, heads-down movement patterns. What began as memory-based prompts became present-moment reflections once early deployments revealed a dramatic jump in participation. Across Union Square, a crosswalk, and an elevator waiting area, we turned hundreds of strangers into storytellers, showing how one object can transform anonymous public space into a site of shared connection.
overview.disciplines: Design Ethnography, Provotyping, Public Installation Deployment, Interactive Prompt Design, Research-Through-Design Methods, Behavioral Field Observation, Sense-Making.

problemContext.problem: Dense cities like New York present a paradox: residents often feel deeply isolated despite living near millions of people, and 52 percent regularly report feeling lonely. This urban anonymity shows up in ordinary avoidance behaviors, headphones in, eyes down, minimal acknowledgment, normalized as simply how city life works. Transitional spaces like crosswalks, subway platforms, and elevator lobbies sit entirely unused as real opportunities for connection. Traditional community-building relies on formal events or costly infrastructure changes that overlook how spontaneously people actually move. The real gap sat between physical proximity and social connection, and finding the moments people were genuinely open to interruption, without disrupting how they navigate the city at all.
problemContext.brought: I conducted field research with the team, mapping movement patterns and behaviors across several New York City locations to inform the interactive urban interventions we designed. I co-created and deployed the Memory Tube installations, iterating prompts and physical designs between phases to steadily lift participation. I also partnered with cross-disciplinary peers to capture and synthesize the stories, observations, and insights we gathered.

accordion.title: Baseline Information
accordion.body: Urban anonymity showed up everywhere we looked: headphones in, eyes down, minimal acknowledgment between strangers who passed each other daily. Fifty-two percent of New Yorkers reported regular loneliness despite constant physical proximity to millions of people. Transitional spaces like crosswalks, subway platforms, and park benches sat unused as connection opportunities, since traditional community-building relied on formal events rather than spontaneous urban movement itself.

accordion.title: Research & Strategy
accordion.body: Grounded in Frayling's research-through-design approach, we treated the design process itself as our method of investigation rather than a step that follows research. Using HMW matrices and a Wheel of Reasoning framework, we mapped three provotype directions, Wait and Play, Memory Landmarks, and Common Enemy, evaluating each for feasibility, impact, and ethics before selecting Memory Landmarks as our primary direction.

accordion.title: Summary of Findings
accordion.body: Shifting our prompt from memory-based to present-focused tripled participation, showing people share immediate emotions more readily than recalled ones in busy urban contexts. A curiosity-participation gap emerged: many stopped and read the prompt but few actually spoke into the tube. Each participant who engaged inspired two to three others to follow, and making our recording equipment visible built trust rather than deterring people.

accordion.title: Defining Design KPI's
accordion.body: Three measures anchored our evaluation as this provotype evolved. Engagement Jump tracked the tripled participation rate once we shifted from memory-based to present-moment prompts. Positive Responses tracked the share of authentic, positive emotional reactions participants shared into the tube. Interaction Time tracked median engagement duration, our proxy for how deeply a stranger actually connected with the installation.

accordion.title: Prototyping & Implementation Strategy
accordion.body: Implementation moved through two deployment phases rather than one big launch. Phase one tested a memory-based prompt across three locations, yielding rich observations about curiosity without much direct participation. Phase two refined the prompt to a present-moment question at Union Square, experimenting with recording-equipment visibility and producing dramatically higher engagement and a wider range of emotional expression. Real "Sense Making" synthesis wall (confirmed accurate) — the team's own post-it and photo synthesis of field observations from the Union Square deployment. Real "Integrated Methodology" summary (confirmed accurate) — the team's own four-phase research framework, from Urban Needs Analysis through Sense Making.

artifacts.intro: HMW matrices, a Wheel of Reasoning, and phase-mapped synthesis turned messy fieldwork into direction.

desktopMotion.body: Field documentation shows passersby noticing the golden tube, pausing to read its prompt, circling it slowly with companions, then some finally leaning in to speak their own reflection aloud.

metrics.label: Engagement Jump
metrics.note: Present-moment prompts tripled real participation over memory-based prompts here.

metrics.label: Positive Responses
metrics.note: Participants shared authentic, positive emotional reactions into the tube.

metrics.label: Interaction Time
metrics.note: Median engagement lasted long enough for a genuine exchange.

reflection.body: Shifting our prompt from a memory-based question to a present-moment one worked: asking strangers how they felt right now instead of asking them to recall the past tripled participation, revealing that busy urban contexts reward immediate emotional honesty over quiet reflection. Watching each engaged participant inspire two or three others to follow told me that collective joy spreads through visible permission, not private invitation extended one wary stranger at a time. If I could revisit one decision, I'd have made our recording equipment visible from the very first deployment instead of only the second one, since transparency built real trust we spent our whole first phase assuming we had to hide.
nextSteps: Next, we're collaborating with NYC Parks and transit authorities to expand Memory Tube installations across more boroughs and high-traffic spaces.
We're partnering with community groups to co-create a simple, open-source toolkit for replicating these urban interventions.
We're launching a digital archive to document participant stories and engagement data, and working with city planners to embed these insights into future public space design.
